speakers: Alan Dunn (co-host, rules-based/trend and macro investor; launching Regime Adaptive Fund)
Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged; transcript 'Neil Castro Blast')
summary: Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor Ep.399 (May 2026): Dunn and Kaastrup-Larsen discuss AI and Iran-war supply shocks, trend-following status, Graham Capital's macro-across-monetary-regimes paper and AQR's Jordan Brooks interview. Dunn announces a Regime Adaptive Fund (40% equity / 20% bonds+gold / 40% trend risk). Main conclusions: rate volatility and dispersion drive trend/macro opportunity; trend is a transparent tactical allocation overlay; diversification brings its own periodic pain.

Wealth effect caveat on AI article; data-center geopolitics; UK council elections (chatter)
UK gilts and fiscal risk; immigration and inflation; trend barometer 55; cocoa and fixed income shift in trend followers
Trend index YTD numbers (6 May 2026); AI disinflation to Iran-war stagflation narrative; rate shock hit steepener trades; energy trends offset

AI as positive supply shock vs demand-side capex; 1990s Greenspan analogy; both shocks together; fiscal response bias
Fiscal dominance; China 2000s deflation, AI energy use; stagflation and AI adoption; military spending; Graham Capital papers introduced
Graham paper: macro alpha vs monetary policy activity, dispersion, easing/tightening regimes
Dispersion favourable; role of inflation stability; 1982-99 vs 2010s for trend; carry and steep curve
Rate volatility as driver of trend opportunity; equities since 2009 not where trend made money; AQR Jordan Brooks portfolio construction as constrained optimisation
Strategic vs tactical allocation; trend as TAA; insurance-like profile; inflation types vs bonds, equities, commodities
Discomfort of diversification; March 2026 rate shock vs 2022; drawdowns correct prior gains

Stay-invested message critique; trend embeds a course of action; fund vol 10-12%; equity buoyancy dilemma
Flows and positioning dominate macro; trend suited to non-predictive; sign-off and disclaimers

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the AI economy in in the grew in the US grew by 31% in Q1 but the non-AI economy was basically flat
claims.claim: AI-related capex is distorting US growth data so aggregate GDP overstates breadth of the economy, complicating policy reads.
claims.indicator: AI economy vs non-AI economy growth (Q1 2026)
claims.testable: partly: depends on how AI economy is defined

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: Q1 earnings on on on on track to be up 27%. But the Mag 7 to be up 61% and the rest uh just up 16%.
claims.claim: Index earnings growth is heavily concentrated in the Magnificent 7, so headline earnings overstate broad profit growth.
claims.indicator: Q1 2026 earnings growth: S&P vs Mag 7 vs rest

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the percentage that wages account for in total output fell to 54% uh in in Q1 and that was the lowest since uh records began in 1947
claims.claim: Labor share of output fell to a record low 54%, consistent with AI/capital-intensive growth shifting income from wages to capital.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: 33 counties account for 72% of the data centers
claims.claim: Data-center construction is geographically concentrated, so an AI capex unwind would hit construction employment less broadly than headline spending implies.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: he didn't talk about what would happen to the stock market and the possible wealth effect from that
claims.claim: An AI bust would not be benign for the economy because falling equity prices would hit consumption via the wealth effect, which the 'little impact' argument ignores.
claims.direction: consumption down if AI equities unwind

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you suddenly realize that you've put you know an important data center in a region that is not as stable as you would have thought
claims.claim: Geopolitical conflict exposes AI infrastructure concentration in unstable regions, adding a risk channel for AI-linked assets.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: as yields go up that you know takes in takes more money to to service the debt and and and the risk is you get a a vicious uh cycle
claims.claim: Rising government bond yields raise debt-service costs and can start a vicious cycle, so political shifts that raise fiscal risk can pressure gilts.
claims.direction: long gilts down when yields spike
claims.conditions: after the Truss-type episode; markets calmed after the election result
claims.testable: partly: yield and fiscal-risk events testable

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: we we need immigration to to boost the labor force to you know long-term growth as a function of productivity and labor force growth
claims.claim: Restricting immigration cuts labor-force growth and creates labor shortages that push up inflation, so social and economic policy goals conflict.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: My own trend barometer finished yesterday at 55.
claims.claim: The host's trend barometer at 55 signals still-strong trend conditions across markets, consistent with this year's trend performance.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Coco has found some uh uh revised uh energy to the upside and and that's probably hurting trend followers right now because of the uh longer term trend that it's been in to the downside
claims.claim: A sharp counter-trend rebound in cocoa hurts trend followers who are positioned short after a long downtrend.
claims.direction: trend followers lose on short cocoa

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's been a somewhat decisive shift from Q4 to now uh in terms of not only reducing long exposure, but
claims.claim: Trend followers have moved from long to short fixed income since Q4 2025, positioning for an inflationary world.
claims.conditions: if inflation narrative holds; may need to reverse

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Uh the stock CT index down seven basis points but up 10.14% so far this year.
claims.claim: SG CTA-type trend indices were up roughly 10% YTD by 6 May 2026, versus S&P 500 total return 7.59%, showing trend is outperforming equities this year.
claims.indicator: trend indices YTD (SG Trend, CTA, Short-term traders)

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Coco by far the biggest one, up 23% so far in May.
claims.claim: Cocoa was the largest month-to-date mover in May 2026 (+23%), a counter-trend move.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: it became very apparent quickly that the central bankers couldn't be cutting rates uh in an environment where energy prices were spiraling higher
claims.claim: An energy price spike from the Iran war removed the disinflation-driven rate-cut narrative, since central banks cannot cut into rising energy-driven inflation.
claims.indicator: energy prices vs rate cut expectations
claims.direction: front-end yields up, curve steepener trades lose

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: a lot of uh funds across macro or V uh had steepen their positions on effectively betting on on lower short-term rates
claims.claim: Crowded curve-steepener positions betting on lower short rates amplified the rate shock when energy prices spiked.
claims.conditions: when short-rate cut expectations are repriced

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: you had the trends in the energy
claims.claim: Trend followers were offset in the rate shock by strong energy trends, so cross-asset breadth cushions losses in one sector.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: only 12 months ago you were trying to explain the the poor performance of trend by reference to some random factors.
claims.claim: Narratives explaining trend performance are post hoc; strong runs are impossible to anticipate but do recur, so one should not time trend allocations on stories.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: conflict like that which pushes up oil prices is what economists call an adverse supply shock
claims.claim: An oil-price spike from Middle East conflict is an adverse supply shock (aggregate supply shifts left), producing stagflationary pressure that hurts both bonds and equities.
claims.direction: bonds and equities down in real terms

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the big period of stagflation was the 1970s and we saw negative real returns for bonds and equities
claims.claim: In the 1970s stagflation both bonds and equities had negative real returns, so a stagflation regime breaks the 60/40 diversification.
claims.indicator: real returns of bonds and equities in 1970s

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: The European Central Bank raised rates in May of 2008
claims.claim: In 2008 the ECB hiked into an oil spike and was cutting by year-end, showing central banks can mis-respond to energy shocks.
claims.conditions: oil-driven inflation coinciding with a downturn

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the classic response is to look through it because they won't necessarily generate second order effects as economists call it
claims.claim: Central banks normally look through energy shocks unless they spill into second-round effects.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: people are more sensitive to higher prices at the moment because we had the experience of inflation uh during co
claims.claim: After the COVID inflation, households are more price-sensitive, raising the risk that inflation expectations de-anchor after an energy shock and limiting central banks' ability to look through.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: Obviously the US is probably more insulated to the shock than than Europe or or Asia.
claims.claim: An oil shock has asymmetric geographic effects; the US (net energy exporter) is more insulated than Europe or Asia, so shocks drive FX and relative equity moves.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: lower income households are disproportionately impacted because gas is going to be a a bigger percentage of their budget
claims.claim: Energy price spikes hit lower-income households hardest because fuel is a larger budget share, weighing on consumption and building pressure for subsidies.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: AI is exactly the opposite in the sense that in theory it pushes the aggregate supply curve out
claims.claim: AI is a positive supply shock, raising output at lower cost, so in theory disinflationary and a case for rate cuts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: this parallel between this productivity boost that AI will give and the productivity boom that we saw in the 1990s
claims.claim: Fed chair candidate Walsh and the administration use a 1990s new-economy analogy to justify lower rates on AI productivity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: by the end of the decade um he was raising rates and that's because there's not just a supply element to this uh uh productivity shock
claims.claim: In the 1990s Greenspan eventually hiked because productivity booms also generate a demand boom from investment, so AI capex is an inflationary impulse that offsets the supply disinflation.
claims.conditions: when capex demand outpaces supply gains

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: maybe over a trillion dollars uh of of capex spending uh next year
claims.claim: Hyperscaler AI capex is approaching $1 trillion a year and rising, a very real demand impulse.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: don't think we've had a shock or a period where we've had both of these shocks at the same time
claims.claim: Simultaneous positive supply (AI) and negative supply (energy) shocks have no historical precedent, making policy and model-based inference especially uncertain.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: you know they both play into this tendency for more and more spending in response to any kind of shock
claims.claim: Both shocks bias governments toward more spending (subsidies, defence, AI-displacement support) at a time of high debt, adding fiscal pressure.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: inching towards fiscal dominance continues to be one of the big themes and trends
claims.claim: Rising spending pressure is pushing economies toward fiscal dominance, a key macro theme.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: China became the production hub of everything, right? is massively deflationary
claims.claim: China becoming the world's production hub in the 2000s was a bigger disinflationary force than AI probably is.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's also very energyheavy in terms of consumption
claims.claim: AI is energy-intensive, so during an energy supply shock its disinflationary efficiency gains may be offset by higher energy demand.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: a stagflationary impulse from from higher energy prices and an economic downturn, I mean that could accentuate or accelerate AI adoption
claims.claim: A downturn from higher energy prices could accelerate AI adoption and job losses as firms cut costs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's nothing to say that equity markets can't do well in an inflationary uh period
claims.claim: Equities can do well in inflationary periods until interest rates rise enough to bite, so what matters is the policy rate response.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: macro alpha is higher for more activity
claims.claim: Graham Capital finds macro alpha is higher when central banks are more active (more hikes and cuts), because rate volatility creates opportunity for macro traders.
claims.indicator: number of rate hikes and cuts vs macro alpha
claims.conditions: especially when hikes or cuts reach double digits
claims.testable: yes: Graham paper on macro across monetary regimes

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: different cycles across different economies um will will also tend to generate opportunities not just in in interest rate markets but also I guess in currency markets
claims.claim: Divergence in monetary-policy cycles across countries creates opportunities in rates and FX for macro.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: macro tends to do better um before hikes uh relative to a 60/40 portfolio
claims.claim: Macro outperforms 60/40 in the period before rate hikes, as markets price in hikes and 60/40 suffers while rate volatility creates fixed income opportunities.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the macro tended to do better in post a cut as opposed to a pre-cut
claims.claim: Macro performs better after a cut than before one.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: easing cycles are obviously um typically recessionary periods
claims.claim: Macro and trend do especially well in easing cycles because they are typically recessions, which cause repricing and strong trends across markets.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the 2010s was a was a tough period for macro
claims.claim: The 2010s were tough for macro because there was little dispersion across economies.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: generally dispersion is is a theme that that that that seen as favorable for for hedge funds and macro in general
claims.claim: Greater dispersion in rates and economies favours macro hedge funds; recent Fed/ECB/BOJ/UK divergence has been such an opportunity.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the period between 1982 and 1999, 17 years, was by far the strongest
claims.claim: The host's 50-plus-year trend track record was strongest in 1982-1999, a period of unstable (not high) inflation and moderate rates, while 2010-2018 with low rates and very stable inflation was hardest, suggesting inflation instability matters.
claims.conditions: unstable inflation helps trend; stable low inflation hurts

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you had not only low interest rates, but you had very stable inflation
claims.claim: The 2010s challenge for trend and macro came from both zero rates and very stable inflation, not just from rate policy direction.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: when rates start to come down that creates very strong opportunities obviously in fixed income because you start to see a bit a trend
claims.claim: When rates are high and start falling, fixed income trends are strong and a steep yield curve also gives good carry.
claims.conditions: after high rates start to fall

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: good carry when the yield curve is very steep
claims.claim: A steep yield curve provides carry for long fixed-income positions.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: it's really uh the volatility and the magnitudes of the moves in in interest rates that tends to be from my perspective the the main driver of of the opportunity set for trend and and and for macro
claims.claim: Interest-rate volatility and the size of rate moves are the main driver of trend and macro opportunity.
claims.testable: yes: rate vol vs trend returns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: that's not where trend followers have made any money really uh compared to other sectors
claims.claim: A big equity bull market since 2009 did not make trend followers much money because trending equity exposure is hard to capture versus buy-and-hold; optics deceive.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: market rates in the longer end is actually gone up
claims.claim: After the Fed began cutting, longer-end yields rose, so inflation expectations can matter more than the short end for market opportunity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the more you know the varied sources of of investment opportunity you use that increases your opportunity set
claims.claim: Per AQR's Jordan Brooks, portfolio construction is optimisation of objectives under constraints, and broader investable universe raises the opportunity set.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: whereas if you introduce long short strategies that in that that brings in more flexibility
claims.claim: Allowing long-short and leverage (return stacking) adds flexibility versus long-only multi-asset portfolios.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: they go from 60% equities to 57% equities. Big deal.
claims.claim: Conventional tactical asset allocation tilts are marginal (e.g. 60 to 57 equities) with little portfolio impact.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: one of the most powerful and transparent approaches to tactical assets allocation is trend following
claims.claim: Trend following is a simple, transparent, systematic tactical asset allocation that modulates bond and equity exposure and adds currencies and commodities.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: it has obviously had some of its best periods of performance in equity bear markets
claims.claim: Trend has behaved insurance-like with its best periods in equity bear markets but, unlike insurance, has a positive long-term return.
claims.indicator: trend returns in equity bear markets

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: bond markets tend to do badly with both core higher core inflation and higher uh food and energy inflation
claims.claim: Bonds fall with both core and food-and-energy inflation.
claims.indicator: core vs food and energy inflation

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: equities, according to his research, can do fine with uh food and energy price inflation, but tend to struggle with higher core inflation like we saw in 2022
claims.claim: Equities tolerate food-and-energy inflation but struggle with higher core inflation, as in 2022.
claims.indicator: core vs food and energy inflation

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: commodities tend to do better um with higher um food and energy inflation
claims.claim: Commodities benefit from food-and-energy inflation, being closest to those goods.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: if you have equities and bonds you're effectively um you're short inflation risk essentially
claims.claim: A stock-bond portfolio is short inflation risk, so trend and commodities are needed as an inflation hedge.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: there can be a discomfort of diversification
claims.claim: Even well-diversified portfolios occasionally lose in all components at once by chance, as in March 2026 and 'death by a thousand cuts'; this is not a construction failure.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: we had a raid shock back in 2022 and many of those strategies did well just by virtue of initial positioning
claims.claim: Whether trend and macro profit from a rate shock depends on initial positioning, so identical shocks can yield opposite results (March 2026 loss vs 2022 gain).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: you are basically substituting one type of pain for another type of pain
claims.claim: Diversifying to avoid large equity bear markets or a lost decade means accepting periodic simultaneous losses.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we corrected a small amount of uh the last six months returns and then we went straight back uh uh in April and made new all-time highs
claims.claim: Trend drawdowns often only correct prior gains (March 2026, Feb 2018) before recovering quickly.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's like 30 40 50 plus% draw downs along the way
claims.claim: Market wizards' track records include 30 to 50 percent drawdowns, so large returns require tolerance for discomfort.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe they're kind of capturing flows that the rest of us uh will never see
claims.claim: Medallion and multi-strategy funds' smooth returns may come from market-making and flow capture unavailable to others.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's been an improvement or maybe an better acceptance from from institutional investors
claims.claim: Institutional investors increasingly accept trend drawdowns as part of the strategy; wealth channel is still evolving.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: stacking um trend with um with say equities or bonds
claims.claim: Return stacking (trend on top of equities or bonds) was popularised after 2020 to bring trend to wealth investors.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: trend exposure in an asset class is very different to that asset class return because you're going long and short
claims.claim: Trend in an asset class is a different premium from the asset's own beta, so trend should trade equities even when stacked on equity beta.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: it stems from behavioral biases etc.
claims.claim: The trend premium stems from behavioral biases and is better when applied across many markets.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: what you're doing with having trend is you're modulating the equity exposure as well uh as as being a diversifier
claims.claim: Trend in equities modulates equity exposure on top of diversifying.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's part of the correlation matrix that many managers um apply and it may from time to time simply allow us to take either more or less risk in other parts of the portfolio
claims.claim: Excluding equities from trend would change the correlation matrix and risk budget, reducing capacity for bond exposure that can add returns.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: You've got a strategic asset allocation plus a tactical asset allocation plus some additional trend exposure to currencies
claims.claim: SAA + trend + currency and commodity trend yields a regime-adaptive portfolio.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's your best ideas product you shouldn't try and constrain it uh as much as I know that some people do because of commercial reasons
claims.claim: An unconstrained trend program is the best-ideas product; researchers generally do not want to constrain design, including equity exposure.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: constrained to long only uh you know short inflation risk underallocated to commodities underallocated to tactical strategies
claims.claim: Vanilla multi-asset funds are long-only, short inflation risk, and lack tactical strategies, so cannot respond to correlation or structural shifts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: The challenge for investors is always the behavioral challenge of holding these strategies because as we've been saying the returns can come in lumps
claims.claim: Investors struggle to hold trend because returns come in lumps with periods of underperformance; embedding it in one portfolio reduces that behavioral risk.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: terms I think in terms of 40% of portfolio risk is to growth assets or equities 20% of portfolio risk to diversifying assets uh bonds and gold and then 40% of portfolio risk is to trend following
claims.claim: The Regime Adaptive Fund allocates risk 40% growth, 20% diversifiers (bonds/gold) and 40% trend following, sized by volatility and medium-term correlations.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the equity beta fluctuates quite a lot from you know in excess of one to to negative at times
claims.claim: With a large trend sleeve the portfolio's equity beta ranges from above one to negative, creating meaningful tactical tilts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: It will protect you at times. It will provide benefits at times that like historically we've seen that 2022 2008 etc.
claims.claim: Trend overlay protects in 2008 and 2022 but costs in choppy markets.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: that pairing of um tactical uh trading from trend following with long only uh beta from from equities and from other markets delivers a higher risk adjusted return over time
claims.claim: Pairing trend with long-only beta delivers higher risk-adjusted returns and a built-in adaptation mechanism to structural change.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: The big risk that investors have to worry about is is not a it's not a 2022.
claims.claim: The real risk is a 50 percent equity drawdown or lost decade (2008, 1970s), not short episodes like 2022 or COVID, so a pre-defined response matters.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the fact that trend following embeds a course of action um a series of steps that will be taken to respond to market trends
claims.claim: 'Stay invested' is a weak message; trend embeds a systematic response to major drawdowns.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: yeah about 10 to 12% is is the expectation so about 2/3 of the equity market volatility
claims.claim: Expected volatility of the Regime Adaptive Fund is 10-12%, about two-thirds of equity volatility.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: how do you construct a portfolio to to to to participate if it continues but protect yourself if it doesn't
claims.claim: Equities keep making new highs despite geopolitical risk; investors need participation with protection, which a trend/tactical sleeve provides.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's much more driven by flows and positioning and and and and and all sorts of other things
claims.claim: Markets are increasingly driven by flows and positioning rather than traditional macro news (e.g. central bank speak).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I actually think this environment lends well to these type of strategies that really
claims.claim: In a flow-driven, deglobalising world non-predictive trend strategies are well suited, though returns may not be massive.
